The Aguaje de Centinela was a spring used by Native Californians, Californios, and early Americans.
The earliest residents of what is now Inglewood were Native Americans who used the Aguaje de Centinela natural springs in today's Edward Vincent Sr. Park.
Local historian Gladys Waddingham wrote that these springs took the name Centinela from the hills that rose gradually around them, which allowed ranchers to watch over their herds.
Much of Inglewood was originally part of Rancho Sausal Redondo, granted in 1837 to Antonio Ygnacio Ávila.
Among the original settlers of Los Angeles in 1781 was Jose Manuel Orchado Machado.
These settlers were ordered by San Gabriel Mission officials to graze their animals on the ocean side of Los Angeles to avoid infringing on mission lands.
The settlers, or pobladores, drove some of their cattle to lush pasture lands near Centinela Springs and built a corral and hut for herders in 1822.
In 1834, Ygnacio Machado built the Centinela Adobe.
Later, Avila constructed a three-room adobe house on a slight rise overlooking the creek that ran from Centinela Springs to the ocean.
The area that is now Inglewood was divided into two rancho grants: Rancho Sausal Redondo and Rancho Aguaje de la Centinela.
In 1834, Ygnacio Machado built the Centinela Adobe on a rise above present-day Interstate 405.
In 1834, Ygnacio Machado was granted Rancho Aguaje de la Centinela.
The Centinela-Inglewood Company put on a four-horse coach between their office and Inglewood in 1887 to carry passengers desiring to see the property.
Arrangements were soon completed for frequent fast trains between Los Angeles and Inglewood over the California Southern Railroad.
Inglewood Park Cemetery was founded in 1905.
The city has been home to Hollywood Park Racetrack from 1938 to 2013, one of the premier horse racing venues in the United States.
Fosters Freeze, the first soft serve ice cream chain in California, was founded by George Foster in Inglewood in 1946.
Inglewood was named an All-America City by the National Civic League in 1989 and again in 2009 for its visible progress.
The Ku Klux Klan had a presence in Inglewood in the 1920s, with the most notable event being the 1922 raid.
The Klan had a chapter in Inglewood as late as October 1931.
Labor troubles became a serious issue during the early years of World War II as local industries supplied the Allies against the wishes of Communist local union officials.
In 1941, the United Auto Workers (UAW) won an election over the International Association of Machinists and represented all employees at North American Aviation in Inglewood.
The UAW demanded a starting pay of 75 cents an hour plus a 10-cent raise for current employees.
The UAW made a no-strike pledge but suddenly called a wildcat strike on June 4, closing the plant that produced a fourth of the nation's fighter planes.
Washington intervened to reopen the plant with approval from national CIO leadership.
When Germany invaded the USSR in late June 1941, Communist activists became strong supporters of war production and crushed wildcat strikes.
"No blacks had ever lived in Inglewood" according to Gladys Waddingham.
By 1960, "they lived in great numbers along its eastern borders," causing displeasure among the predominantly white residents already residing in Inglewood.
In 1960, the census counted only 29 "Negroes" among Inglewood's 63,390 residents.
Not a single black child attended the city's schools.
Real-estate agents refused to show homes to blacks.
A rumored curfew kept blacks off the streets at night.
In 1965, the Inglewood school board was aware of a growing influx of black families into its eastern areas but did nothing about it.
In 1969, an organization called "Morningside Neighbors" changed its name to "Inglewood Neighbors" in hopes of promoting more integration.
On July 22, 1970, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Max F. Deutz ordered Inglewood schools to desegregate in response to a suit filed by 19 parents.
At least since 1965, the Inglewood school board had been aware of a growing influx of black families into its eastern areas but did nothing about it.

On August 31, 1970, Judge Deutz rejected an appeal by four parents who said the school board was not responsible for segregation; they claimed blacks "selected their places of residence by voluntary choice."
The first black principal among the 18 Inglewood schools was Peter Butler at La Tijera Elementary in 1971.
In 1972, Curtis Tucker Sr. became the first black city council member.
That year, composer LeRoy Hurte, an African-American, took the baton of the Inglewood Symphony Orchestra and continued to work with it for 20 years.
Edward Vincent Jr. became Inglewood's first black mayor in 1983.
In that decade, whites left the city in increasing numbers, and Inglewood became the first city in California to declare Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday a holiday.
The 1990 census showed that Latinos in Inglewood had increased by 134% since 1980, the largest jump in the South Bay.
Economic factors played a role in where new arrivals settled.
Housing was generally less expensive here than elsewhere.
Real-estate agents reported receiving a warmer welcome from residents.
The white population dropped from nearly 21% in 1980 to 8.5% in 1990.
In the 2000 census, blacks made up 47% of the city's residents (53,060 people).
Latinos comprised 46% (51,829) of the population.
The Census Bureau estimated that in 2007, the percentage of blacks had declined to 41% (48,252), and Latinos were at 52.5% (61,847).
The white population declined from 19% (21,505) to 17.7% (20,853).
That year, only one of the city's five city council members was Latino: Jose Fernandez.
No Latinos were on the five-member board of education.
In 2007, the area served by the Inglewood post office had 98 churches, temples, mosques, chapels and other houses of worship.
The first church service was held in April 1888 at the Inglewood House hotel on Commercial Street (today's La Brea Avenue).
Later, services were in Bucephalus Hall but eventually moved to Hyde Park.
In 1907, a group of Episcopalians began services in a private home.
A few years later, the first Catholic services were held in Bank Hall.

In 1910, the Presbyterians moved their two buildings, a sanctuary and a manse, to the corner of Grevillea and Nutwood because the streetcars on Market Street were so noisy and threw dust and sand fleas into windows.
In 2018, an investigation began into a 2012 trash-hauling contract valued at $100 million; it went to a bidder with connections to current mayor James T. Butts.
The bidder, Consolidated Disposal Services, secured the contract soon after hiring Michael Butts, brother of Mayor Butts, as an operations manager.
Consolidated continues to provide garbage collection services as of 2023.
According to the United States Census Bureau, Inglewood has a total area of 9.1 square miles (24 km²).
Downtown Inglewood is 4.15 miles (6.68 km) from Los Angeles International Airport.
It is part of the Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim metropolitan statistical area.

Inglewood consists of 10 neighborhoods that are indicated by symbols on street signs: Morningside Park, Downtown Inglewood, Fairview Heights, Arbor Village, Hollypark Knolls, Centinela Heights, Century Heights, Inglewood Knolls, and Lockhaven.
The Crenshaw-Imperial district was a later annexation to Inglewood, California. It has its own branch public library and an important shopping center for the area.
Morningside Park is a commercial district in the eastern part of the city.

Though the city of Inglewood does not define the district's boundaries, it may be delineated by Hyde Park on the north, Manchester Square on the east, Century Boulevard on the south, and Prairie Avenue on the west.
The major streets that run through the area are Manchester and Crenshaw boulevards.
It is six miles (10 km) from Los Angeles International Airport and about two miles (3 km) from SoFi Stadium.
The district is also the location of Kia Forum, an entertainment venue where for 32 years the NBA's Los Angeles Lakers and NHL's Los Angeles Kings played.
The Village at Century shopping center is located in this neighborhood.
This neighborhood was once the site of the Hollywood Park Racetrack.
It is home to three gated communities: Carlton Square, Briarwood Village & The Renaissance.
North Inglewood is a neighborhood north of the former Santa Fe railroad tracks where the K Line currently is.
In 2009, it was reported to be the site of a "burgeoning arts scene" at East Hyde Park Boulevard and La Brea Avenue.
Fairview Heights is a signed area north of Florence and east of La Brea Avenues.
Inglewood Knolls is situated in the southeastern corner of the city.
It is bordered by Crenshaw Blvd. on the west, 108th St. on the north, Spinning Ave. on the east, and Imperial Highway on the south.
A shopping center was constructed on the northeastern quadrant of the intersection of Crenshaw and Imperial in the mid-1950s.
Century Park Elementary School is located on Spinning Ave., although fully within Inglewood city limits, it is part of the L.A. school district.
Climate data for Inglewood shows average temperatures ranging from 18.4°C to 24.6°C in summer and 13.0°C in winter.
The 2020 United States Census reported that Inglewood had a population of 107,762.

The racial makeup of Inglewood was 50.6% Hispanic or Latino (of any race), 43.9% African American, 23.3% White (2.9% non-Hispanic White), 0.7% Native American, 1.5% Asian, 26.3% from other races, and 4.1% from two or more races.
The Census reported that 98.6% of the population lived in households, 0.9% lived in non-institutionalized group quarters, and 0.5% were institutionalized.

Of the 36,389 households, 42.1% had children under living in them, 36.0% were married couples living together, 24.7% had a female householder with no husband present, 8.1% had a male householder with no wife present, 6.4% were unmarried partnerships, 0.6% were same-sex partnerships, 25.7% were made up of individuals, and 7.6% had someone living alone who was 65 or older.
The average household size was 2.97. With 25,019 families (68.8% of all households), the average family size was 3.59.
The age distribution was 26.7% under 18, 10.8% from 18 to 24, 28.9% from 25 to 44, 24.3% from 45 to 64, and 9.4% who were 65 or older.
The median age was 33.4 years. For every 100 females, there were 90.6 males. For every 100 females 18 and over, there were 86.8 males.
The 38,429 housing units had an average density of 4,226.5/sq mi (1,631.9/km²), of which 37.0% were owner-occupied and 63.0% were occupied by renters.
The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.5%; the rental vacancy rate was 5.5%, while 39.2% of the population lived in owner-occupied housing units and 59.4% lived in rental housing units.
According to the 2020 United States Census, Inglewood had a median household income of $43,394, with 22.4% of the population living below the federal poverty line.
Mexican and Salvadoran are common ancestries in Inglewood.
Mexico and El Salvador were the most common foreign places of birth in the 2000 census.

In 2009, the Los Angeles Times's "Mapping L.A." project supplied these neighborhood statistics based on the 2000 census: The population was 112,482, or 12,330 people per square mile, among the highest densities for the South Bay and among the highest densities for the county.
The percentage of African Americans was high for the county, and the population was moderately diverse.
Median household income was $46,574, low for both the South Bay and for the county.
The median age was 29, young for the county; the percentage of residents aged 10 or under was among the county's highest.
Three people on average lived in each household – high for the South Bay but about average for the county.
There was a higher percentage of families headed by single parents than elsewhere in the county.
The percentage of veterans who served during 1975–89 and 1990–99 was among the county's highest.
In 2022, Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority's Greater Los Angeles Homeless Count counted 751 homeless individuals in Inglewood.

Kia Forum, built in 1967, is an indoor arena designed by architect Charles Luckman to evoke the Roman Forum. It was one of LA's biggest concert venues for decades and hosted the NBA's Los Angeles Lakers and NHL's Los Angeles Kings until 1999 when they moved to Staples Center.

In 2012, the Forum was purchased by The Madison Square Garden Company for $23.5 million; MSG announced plans to spend $50 million to refurbish and renovate the arena for use as a "world-class" concert venue.
The "Fabulous" Forum presented by Chase reopened on January 15, 2014, with the first of six historic performances by the Eagles.
On April 4, 2022, "The Forum" was renamed "Kia Forum" due to a naming rights deal between Steve Ballmer and car manufacturer Kia.
In 2016, construction began on SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. It opened in 2020 and hosted Super Bowl LVI in 2022 and will host Super Bowl LXI in 2027.
SoFi Stadium also hosts the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2028 Summer Olympics.
The Southeast Symphony Association is a non-profit, musical and cultural association in Inglewood founded in 1948 to create an orchestra that welcomes African-American musicians.
The annual Open Studios event features "drawing, painting, photography and more," organized by a volunteer group of artists with support from the Inglewood Cultural Arts, Inc. (ICA) organization.
Inglewood is home to the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers of the National Football League who play at SoFi Stadium.
The Los Angeles Lakers and Los Angeles Kings played their home games at Kia Forum from 1967 to 1999 until they moved to Crypto.com Arena in Downtown Los Angeles.

On July 26, 2019, the Los Angeles Clippers announced plans to build a new arena and entertainment center in Inglewood. The project includes an arena, team's business and basketball offices, training facility, community and retail spaces.
The privately financed project was expected to be completed at the same time their current leasing agreement with Crypto.com Arena is set to expire.

On September 10, 2019, Clippers owner Steve Ballmer announced plans to invest $100 million into Inglewood as part of the arena deal. The investment includes $80 million for affordable housing and assistance to renters and first-time homebuyers, and another $12.75 million invested into school and youth programs.
The new arena opened in August 2024.
SoFi Stadium will host several matches during the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
Inglewood has a council–city manager type of government with the mayor as the chief executive officer but an equal member of the city council.
The current mayor is James T. Butts Jr., who took office after unseating Daniel K. Tabor, who completed the term of Roosevelt Dorn.
The Inglewood Police Department is the city's police department.
Since the Inglewood Fire Department was disbanded in 2000, the city contracts its fire service with the Los Angeles County Fire Department.
